That's so stupid. I'm a programmer, and I tried to teach some really smart people programming - and they couldn't do it. You need the ability to imagine and visualize complex data structures, relations between data, program flow and algorithms. You can be highly intelligent without having this ability, and then you will never be a decent programmer, regardless how much an AI supports you. By the way, there were so many proposals to make "everyone" a programmer: Expert system, code generators, visual programming, imitating natural languages (e.g. SQL), domain specific languages, the list goes on, and nothing so far had an widespread impact to non-programmers. E.g. you can do a lot of programming in Excel, it's dead easy and accessible for like 20 years, and still very few people use this potential for more than a few snippets copied from the internet. I'm a Java programmer, and I can tell you the one thing that got kids into Java programming. It was nothing "convenient", is was nothing made for non-programmers, nope, the main thing which was attracting kids to Java programming was... Minecraft.

I really hope your optimism comes true. For our children. The difference between all previous job replacements and AI is that all prior tech did one job at a time, tech was invented to optimize and eventually remove person from the task process. And at all these points tech took the simple, repetitive and boring part of the job, the intellectual part was not. The people operating the tech had to become more intellectual and knowledgeable to operate it. Not AI. AI takes the intellectual part, and that's why your prior statistics cannot project on the future. Can you imagine pilot asking AI what to do in complicated situation (roof flies off)? I hope not. But that's what programmers, software architects and even security experts are now doing. Why? Because people are lazy and AI does a good enough job. Apps, articles, books, videos, ads, images - it all has (currently) lower quality than skilled people but it gets the job done (clicks, views, sales) at fraction of cost and so we get stupider, lower quality content and we consume it and AI learns from it on next iteration. And that's not even that scary that it will take some jobs, it's scary because 90% of people will get stupider relying on it and no clue what next generation will be.

I got my first computer in the 80s. As I saw it advancing, I understood that automation was going to really advance quickly and started thinking about what would happen to jobs. But I knew this wasn't a new idea. There was even a Twilight Zone story about robots taking jobs, and a manager being happy, until a robot replaced that manager at the end. (Sorry for the spoiler.) This fear of lost jobs is an old one. We even have the old folk hero John Henry who outpaced a steam drill in the late 1800s. A story that became very popular. A story spread because it was about automation, and the fear of jobs being taken away. The ATM story has been with me for a while. I got my first ATM card about the same time I got my first computer. And I never saw the teller jobs go away. But I believe I understand AI really well now. At least its impact on society. And unlike this video, I do believe we will lose a lot of jobs. But for the opposite reason. So many people will find out that they can make money with AI, or start a business they never could have before, and quit their jobs.

Solid video. Full stack project owner for several months now, very first. My background education is in data analytics, minimal prior coding experience. My thoughts on “Agent Driven Development” or whatever it’s called: although learning from the top down was tough, I can’t stress enough the value in actually learning the system architecture, learning code quality improvements, the bug fixes etc. It’s what made the difference in successfully deploying the project I worked on. Drilling down to the line by line code is something I’m working on, and I see as an added capacity multiplier. The demand to produce with AI has gone up but if you’re actually taking the time to learn, critique, optimize, and cleanup the codebase you ultimately still end up taking a while to develop. Prompting itself, and knowledge base curation is intensive too, and leans on your own understanding. AI is not magic. Ig the learning path has changed but the learners still benefit here.
